notes: West leads the ♠3 against 3NT. South has 8 top tricks (1 spade, given the lead, 2 hearts, 2 diamonds, and 3 clubs). At first glance it appears South will need a favorable break in one of the minors in order to come to 9 tricks.

South receives a break, however, when East plays the ♠A at trick 1 (the contract cannot be made if East ducks). South should unblock his ♠K under East's ♠A! If East returns a heart South must be careful to win this trick in the closed hand. South's remaining spade is led to drive out the ♠Q, establishing 2 spade winners in the dummy with the ♥A as an entry to cash them.
Unblocking the ♠K at trick 1 ensures the contract. This play gives up an immediate spade winner, but ensures that the dummy will be able to win 2 spade tricks later in the play.

notes: West leads the ♥J against 3NT. It seems natural to play the ♥K or ♥Q from dummy, but if South does so the contract will fail on the above layout. East will win the ♥A and return a heart to drive out dummy's remaining honor. As soon as West wins the ♦A he will cash enough heart tricks to defeat the contract.

South can succeed in the above layout by ducking the opening lead in the dummy. If West continues hearts to East's ♥A, East will be out of hearts and the suit will still be stopped when West wins the ♦A. If West switches to clubs instead of continuing hearts at trick 2, South can win in the dummy and knock out the ♦A to establish enough tricks for the contract (4 spades, 3 diamonds, and 2 clubs).

The recommended duck in dummy at trick 1 will work poorly when West was dealt 5 hearts headed by the ♥AJ10 and the ♦A. The ♥J will win the first trick and West will clear hearts. West will later win the ♦A and 2 more heart tricks to defeat the contract.

The above distribution, where ducking the first trick in the dummy leads to defeat, is unlikely as most West players holding 5 hearts to the ♥AJ10 and the ♦A would have overcalled 1♥ after South's 1♦.

The above layout, where ducking at trick 1 is necessary to make the contract, is more likely given West's Pass over 1♦. This makes it correct to duck the opening lead in the dummy. If the East-West hearts are divided 4-3 the recommended play could give up an overtrick, but it will never cost the contract.

If South starts diamonds by laying down the ♦A, he will succeed whenever diamonds are 3-2 or when the ♦K is singleton. If West was dealt 4 diamonds including the ♦K, however, South will be in trouble. Both defenders follow to the first round of diamonds, but West will duck the second round, allowing dummy to win the trick. With the lead locked in the dummy, South has no way to play diamonds for 1 loser and the contract will fail.

The contract has no hope if East was dealt 4 diamonds to the ♦K, but South can succeed when West has 4 diamonds to the ♦K. South should not cash the ♦A at trick 3. He should take advantage of the lead being in his hand and lead a low diamond toward the dummy. West must duck to give the defense any chance and the ♦Q or ♦J is played from dummy.

If East was dealt a singleton ♦K the contract will fail when leading the ♦A would have succeeded. East is much more likely to have a small singleton diamond (as there are 4 small diamonds and only 1 ♦K) and in this case dummy will win the trick.

A diamond is then played to the ♦A, leaving South well placed to lead a second diamond toward the dummy. West will be held to a single diamond trick. When West is unable to cash more than 2 spade tricks the contract will be made.

When West follows with the ♥K, South's only problem becomes avoiding 2 club losers. By double finessing in clubs South will usually be able to lose only 1 club trick, but if West has both the ♣K and ♣Q this plan will not work. South can guarantee the contract regardless of the distribution of the missing club honors by playing for an elimination.

South should strip all of the spades and diamonds from both hands before playing clubs. The ♦K is cashed and a diamond is played to dummy's ♦A. Dummy's remaining diamond is ruffed by South, eliminating that suit. South then eliminates spades by leading to dummy's ♠K.

The time has come to play clubs. A club is led from dummy and passed to West when East follows small. West is now endplayed. A club return will hold South's club losers to 1 and a diamond or spade return will surrender a ruff and discard. Once again only 1 club trick is lost.

West would win and clear the suit. West would later win a trick with the ♣K and cash the setting trick in spades.

South can guarantee the contract by winning West's heart opening lead with dummy's ♥A. South finesses in clubs, but when West wins the ♣K he cannot attack spades without giving South his 9th trick (South has already won a trick with the ♥A and can win 4 diamond tricks and 3 club tricks).

If West exits passively in a minor, South wins and plays the ♥Q to knock out the ♥K. East's spade return is covered by South and won cheaply by West. South's remaining spades are a stopper, however, as long as West is on lead.

If, instead of switching to a minor after winning the ♣K, West continues hearts, the result is the same. East wins the ♥K to play a spade, but South has his 9 tricks established and a certain stopper in spades (since East cannot gain the lead again).

notes: West leads the ♠5 against 3NT. It seems natural to play a low spade from the dummy in order to guarantee 3 spade tricks, but if South does so he will be sorry. If East has the ♠Q he will force out South's ♠A.
When the ♣Q does not drop under the ♣A and ♣K, South lacks the 2 hand entries required to set up and run the clubs.

South can avoid this problem by winning West's spade opening lead with dummy's ♠K. South does not need 3 spade tricks, but he does need 2 entries to his hand in order to enjoy his long club suit. When the ♣A and ♣K are cashed and the ♣Q has not dropped, South can cross to his hand in spades and force out the ♣Q. The ♦A will act as an entry to South's remaining club winners. Provided that the defense cannot win 4 spade tricks, the contract is assured.

It is a near certainty that spades are no worse than 5-3 given the opening lead of the ♠5. Players generally lead 4th best from a long suit and the ♠4 is the only outstanding spade lower than the ♠5. Therefore, West was dealt no more than 5 spades and South can safely use the ♠A as his first hand entry. It would not be safe to cross the first time in diamonds as it is possible that one of the defenders (most likely East) was dealt a 5-card diamond suit.

South should cross to the dummy at trick 2 and start trump by leading dummy's ♥6. If East ducks, South can win the ♥Q and play a second round of trump to East's ♥A. South will still have to lose a heart trick and a diamond trick, but the contract will be secure.

If East chooses to rise with the ♥A on the first round of the suit, giving up his second natural trump trick, South will still survive. East is welcome to cash the ♦K and give West a diamond ruff, but there will be only 2 trumps outstanding and the ♥K and ♥Q can take care of these.

notes: West leads the ♥K against 7♠. South must ruff West's heart opening lead, but if he ruffs with the ♠2 the contract will fail. South cashes the ♠K and ♠Q, but East's discard on the second round dooms the contract. With the trump suit blocked South has no way to draw trump directly.

South can get around this problem by ruffing with the ♠10 (instead of the ♠2) at trick 1. The ♠K and ♠Q are cashed, but when East discards on the second round, the trump suit is unblocked and South can draw the rest of the trump with the marked finesse against West's ♠J.

All that remains is to play the club suit for no losers. Since all of dummy's trumps have been used to draw trump there is no way for South to ruff out the suit. South should take the percentage play in clubs, finessing against the ♣Q with East. When the finesse wins and both defenders follow to the second round, the clubs will run and the contract will succeed.

notes: West leads the ♣K against 6♥. South wins the ♣A and draws 2 rounds of trump. When West discards on the second round of trump South has a certain trump loser and will have to avoid losing a spade trick in order to make his contract.

In the above layout South can succeed easily by finessing against East's ♠K, but if the ♠K is in West's hand, South's only's chance is that diamonds are 3-2 so that dummy's diamonds can be used to discard South's spade losers. If South is to make use of dummy's diamonds then East's trumps must be extracted first so that East cannot ruff in to stop the run of the suit.

Suppose South continues with his remaining high trump and surrenders a trump trick to East. If East switches to a spade, South will not know what to do. With the ♠K dealt to West and the diamonds 3-2 South must rise with the ♠A to make the contract, but if East has the ♠K and diamonds break 4-1 then South must finesse in spades in order to succeed.

South can solve this problem by cashing the ♦A and ♦K before surrendering a trump trick to East. If either defender discards (or ruffs) on the second round of diamonds, South will know that the spade finesse is required. East can be given his trump trick and the ♦Q can be used as a later entry to finesse against the ♠K with East.

If both defenders follow to the second round of diamonds, there is no reason to risk the spade finesse. South surrenders a trump trick to East. When East returns a spade South now knows to win the ♠A and run the diamonds for 2 spade discards.

The contract will require East to have the ♣K and if East was dealt 4 clubs then South will need 3 dummy entries for 3 club finesses. The ♥K is 1 entry, but the only other possible entries are in the spade suit (South will not be able to use the diamond suit as the defense is about to get the hearts going). West is very likely to have the ♠J and South should plan to finesse against that card to create and extra dummy entry.

East's heart return is won in the dummy and South continues with a successful club finesse. The time has come to finesse West for the ♠J. When that wins South finesses again in clubs. West's discard means that South's unblock of the ♠Q at trick 1 was necessary - a third dummy entry will be required to pick up the clubs and North's ♠A is still available for that purpose.

Note that if South does not play the ♠Q under East's ♠K at trick 1, the contract can no longer be made in the above layout. East's heart return is won in dummy and South finesses in clubs. If South tries to create a third dummy entry by leading his remaining small spade towards dummy for a finesse against the ♠J, West can play the ♠J, forcing dummy's ♠A. West's fine blocking play defeats the contract by denying South the dummy entries required to pick up the club suit.

South must time the play carefully in order to maximize his chances. After winning West's heart opening lead South should lay down the ♦A. This is a safety play against West being dealt a singleton ♦K. South will never require more than 4 diamond tricks for his contract so he can afford to make this play (versus a first round diamond finesse). If the ♦K drops then South can concede a diamond trick to the defense and he will have enough tricks for his contract.

When both defenders follow to the first round of diamonds, but the ♦K does not drop, South should play a club to the dummy and test that suit by playing 2 more rounds. If both defenders follow to 3 rounds of clubs, South's remaining club will be his 7th winner and South can knock out the ♠A to ensure 9 tricks.

If one of the defenders discards on the third round of clubs (or sooner), 2 spades tricks will not be enough for the contract. South will need a favorable diamond lie to get home and the lead is in the right hand to play that suit. The contract will succeed unless East discards, but the contract can never be made if West has 2 diamond stoppers and clubs are 4-2. The recommended line will lead to success whenever it is possible to make the contract.

2 of South's small clubs can be discarded on dummy's ♦A and ♦K and South's remaining club loser can be ruffed in the dummy. It would be a mistake to try to ruff 2 clubs in dummy (if West was dealt 5332 distribution he could ruff the third round of clubs in front of dummy).

It would also be wrong to draw 2 rounds of trump immediately. If East discards on the second round of trump, South will go down when West was dealt a doubleton diamond along with the outstanding trump. South can ruff a club in dummy and cash the top diamonds for club discards. Dummy will then be down to only diamonds and West's ♥J will be promoted into the setting trick.

South can avoid this danger by drawing at most 1 round of trump before ruffing a club in the dummy. Dummy's top diamonds are then cashed for club discards and South can safely return to his hand in hearts to draw the rest of the trump.

South should play a heart to dummy's ♥K at trick 2 and then cross back to his hand in order to lead a low heart toward dummy's ♥J. If West started with 4 hearts to the ♥Q10 he can do no better than to take his ♥Q and force the dummy with a second round of spades. If West discards on the second round of trump, dummy's ♥J will force East's ♥Q. South can win any return and draw the rest of the trump by finessing against East's ♥10. The contract is at risk against some 4-1 heart breaks if South plays the trump suit in any other manner.

If West follows with a small club under South's ♣J, South should cross again in spades in order to lead a heart toward the ♥Q. If East has the ♥A he must duck (or South will have 9 certain winners), allowing South's ♥Q to win the trick. If West was dealt the ♥A he will take South's ♥Q, but as before, West will be unable to effectively attack diamonds. South will have time to develop his 9th trick in clubs before the defense is able to get the diamonds going.

When both defenders follow small, South should cross to the dummy in diamonds and lead a second round of clubs toward the closed hand. When East follows small, South plays the ♣Q or ♣J.

notes: West leads the ♠J against 3NT. There are only 7 top tricks (3 spades, 3 hearts, and the ♣A). South must hope to establish either his own clubs or dummy's diamonds in order to come to 9 tricks.

After winning West's spade opening lead, it would be wrong to play on clubs as the contract would almost certainly fail even if the East-West clubs were divided favorably. The defense would win the second round of clubs and play a second round of spades to South. When South loses the lead again in clubs, the defenders will stop leading spades in order to deny South access to the long clubs in his hand.

Playing on diamonds gives South much better chances. When South leads a small diamond toward dummy and West follows small, South has to decide which diamond to play from dummy. Playing a small diamond (and planning to play the ♦Q on the second round) will succeed whenever West was dealt a doubleton ♦J.

Playing dummy's ♦Q on the first round is better. This play will succeed when East has a doubleton ♦J and when East has a singleton ♦J. When the ♦Q holds, South continues diamonds to drive out one of the top honors. South can win any return, cross to dummy in hearts, and knock out the outstanding diamond stopper. Later, South can reach the dummy in hearts and enjoy the long diamonds.

If West goes up with an honor on the first round of diamonds, South should win the spade return and cross to the dummy in hearts. South should continue by leading the ♦Q from the dummy in the hope that either East was dealt a doubleton ♦J or West was dealt ♦AJ or ♦KJ doubleton.

The percentage play in both spades and clubs involves finessing against the missing Queens. South should attempt to combine his chances in both of these suits. He should cash the Ace and King of one of these suits to see if the Queen drops. If the Queen does not drop he will still have time to finesse in the other suit.

Since North-South have 8 clubs and only 7 spades between them, the ♣Q is more likely to drop doubleton than the ♠Q. South should therefore start by cashing the top clubs. Furthermore, it is correct to cash the ♣A first so that the lead will be in the dummy (to finesse in spades) should the ♣Q remain outstanding. When the spade finesse wins, South can cross to the dummy in hearts, cash dummy's other top heart, and repeat the spade finesse.

Note that it would be a mistake to cash a top spade early in an attempt to guard against a singleton ♠Q with West. The odds of West holding a singleton ♠Q are much less than the odds of East holding 4 or more spades to the ♠Q. Laying down a top spade before crossing to the ♣K would be fatal in the above layout.

Correct technique will allow South to almost always succeed as long as diamonds divide no worse than 4-2. South should win the first trick with the ♣A and cash dummy's top diamonds. A diamond is ruffed in the closed hand (it would not matter if West could overruff with the ♥A) and South exits in clubs.

The defense must win and play 2 rounds of trump to stop South from ruffing his remaining club in the dummy. South can win the second round of trump in the dummy and ruff another diamond. South draws the rest of the trump (in 2 rounds if necessary) and uses dummy's ♠A as an entry to the established diamond winner.

notes: West leads the ♣K against 5♥. West wins the first 2 tricks in clubs and switches to the ♦Q to dummy's ♦A. South's only possible remaining loser is in the spade suit. South should try to get a count on the East-West hands in order to maximize his chances of success against a 4-1 spade break.

South should continue by leading dummy's ♥2 to his hand followed by a middle heart. West has shown at least 5-5 in the minors with his unusual 2NT overcall. If West discards on the second round of hearts, South should play West to have 2155 distribution (or 6-5 in the minors with a singleton ♠J) and play spades from the top.

If West follows to the second round of hearts, he must have 1255 distribution for there to be a chance. South could plan to lead a top spade from the closed hand on the first round of the suit, hoping that West's singleton spade is the ♠J. There is a another plan, however, that offers much better odds, succeeding when West's singleton spade is the ♠9, ♠8, or ♠7.

South should win the second round of trump in the dummy and lead the ♠10, planning to play the ♠6 from the closed hand if East does not cover with the ♠J. When East does play the ♠J, South wins the trick as West follows with the ♠9. South crosses back to the dummy in hearts for a second spade play. East must split his ♠87 (or South would finesse the ♠6) and South wins the trick as West's discard confirms the spade distribution.
South can now play his ♥3 to dummy's ♥4, placing the lead in the correct hand for a third spade finesse against East.

South should ruff West's club opening lead in hand and draw trump, discarding a club from dummy on the third round. South cashes his heart winners and the ♦A before playing a diamond toward the dummy. When West follows small, dummy's ♦Q is played. If West was dealt the ♦K and ducked then the ♦Q will win the trick and South will make an overtrick by discarding his diamonds on the ♥J and ♣A. West can stop the overtrick, but not the contract, by taking his ♦K.

South still has a chance if East wins the ♦Q with the ♦K. If East is out of diamonds he will be forced to give dummy the lead in either hearts or clubs. South will be able to discard his remaining diamond losers on dummy's ♥J and ♣A. Note the importance of keeping the ♣A in dummy for this endplay to operate (which is why it is necessary to ruff West's club opening).

notes: West leads the ♦J against 4♠. South has 2 certain losers in spades and a certain loser in hearts. The only danger to the contract is that the defense is threatening a diamond ruff as West's ♦J lead suggests he was dealt at most 2 diamonds.

If, after winning West's diamond opening lead, South leads a trump, the defense will win and play a second round of diamonds to South as West follows (presumably with his last diamond). It would be a mistake to play a second round of trump now. In the above layout East would win and give West a diamond ruff to defeat the contract.

South can counter this risk by continuing diamonds himself while the ♠6 is still in dummy. If West ruffs then dummy can overruff and South can cross back to his hand to continue drawing trump. West is out of trump so he won't be scoring any diamond ruffs.

If, instead of ruffing, West discards on the third round of diamonds, South should cash his 2 Aces before playing a 4th round of diamonds. Dummy's ♠6 will prevent West from winning the setting trick with a diamond ruff. Regardless of whether West ruffs or discards South will lose only 2 more tricks (the ♠A and a heart) to make his contract.

It would be a mistake to try to run diamonds before playing 1 round of trump. That line would fail in the above layout (and also when East was dealt a singleton ♠A or ♠K). West would ruff the third round of diamonds, forcing dummy to overruff with the ♠6. East would win the first round of trump and give West a diamond ruff to defeat the contract. The recommended line guards against this danger.

notes: West leads the ♠K against 5♣. There is a certain diamond loser. The contract will only fail if 2 heart tricks have to be lost and this will be possible only if West was dealt both the ♥K and the ♥Q. South can improve his chances by playing along elimination lines.

After winning West's spade opening lead with the ♠A, South should lead a middle club to dummy (retaining the ♣2) as both defenders follow. A spade is ruffed high and another middle club is played to dummy. South ruffs another spade high, eliminating that suit. The ♦A is cashed and South exits in diamonds.

If West wins this trick, he will be endplayed. A spade return will concede a ruff and discard, a heart return will hold South's heart losers to 1, and a diamond return will set up a diamond winner in the dummy (South must ruff high if an honor is played). South's club ♣2 can be played to dummy's ♣3 in order to access dummy's diamond winner.

For the defense to have a chance East must win the trick when South exits in diamonds. If East returns a diamond, South can guarantee the contract by discarding a heart. West is welcome to win the trick. As before, North has an extra diamond winner for South's remaining heart loser and the dummy can be reached with the ♣2 to the ♣3.

A diamond return by East is out and a spade return would concede a ruff and discard. East must therefore return a heart. South ducks and West wins the trick. West will have a safe exit card only if he was dealt 3 or 4 small diamonds. Dummy's remaining high diamond should be played and, if East produces the outstanding honor, South can ruff high and cross to dummy with the ♣2 to the ♣3 and fall back on a second heart finesse.

The recommended line of play never loses to the straightforward line of taking 2 heart finesses. The recommended line gains when West has both heart honors and the diamonds are distributed such that the defense cannot avoid being endplayed (the above diamond layout, for example).

notes: West leads the ♠J against 3NT. South has 6 top tricks (2 spade tricks given the lead, 2 heart tricks, and 2 club tricks). At least 2 more tricks will be available in diamonds once the ♦A is driven out and both hearts and clubs offer chances as well. South must time the play carefully in order to maximize his chances of success.

After winning West's spade opening lead, South should cross to the dummy in clubs in order to play a diamond toward the closed hand. There are 2 reasons for playing diamonds in this fashion. First, East might have been dealt a singleton ♦A. Second, East may have been dealt 4 diamonds including the ♦A. In this case East cannot afford to go up with the ♦A and South's ♦Q or ♦J will win the trick.

South should return to the dummy in clubs, noting East's discard. A second small diamond is led from the dummy and, as before, East must duck and allow South to win the trick. If West follows to the second round of diamonds, South can surrender a diamond trick to establish his 9th trick in that suit. When West discards on the second round of diamonds South will have to look elsewhere for his 9th trick.

Had clubs divided 3-2 South could surrender a club trick at this point, but South has learned that clubs are 4-1 so that plan will not work. South's last chance is to duck a heart trick to the defense in the hope that the East-West hearts are 3-3. The defense will play a second round of spades to South. With the favorable layout of the defenders hearts, South can now win 3 tricks in that suit and make the contract.

notes: West leads the ♥3 against 4♠. It looks natural for South to play the ♥J or ♥10 from the dummy, but this play puts the contract at risk when West has 4 spades. East will not cover with the ♥Q, leaving South with no way of avoiding an eventual loser in hearts (along with 3 certain losers between spades and clubs).

2 rounds of trump reveal the 4-1 break and South's best chance is to cash his remaining high spade before surrendering a trump trick to West. The dummy will later gain the lead with the ♦A. The only chance to avoid a heart loser is to play the suit now, but East will cover dummy's card as South wins the trick. As there are no more entries to the dummy for another heart finesse, East will come to a trick in that suit and the contract will fail.

The key to success on this deal is to play the ♥2 from the dummy at trick 1. East plays the ♥9 (following small is no better) and South wins the ♥A or ♥K. South must now play 4 rounds of spades, exhausting the West hand of trump. West exits in diamonds to dummy's ♦A (3 rounds of clubs is no better).

South is now in a position to play the heart suit for no losers. If East covers with the ♥Q, South wins the trick and the rest of the hearts are all high. If East play a small heart instead, the lead will remain in the dummy for another heart finesse. The recommended line allows South to avoid a heart loser, regardless of how East defends.

South should start drawing trump, but when East discards on the second round, South should stop drawing trump. If South makes the mistake of drawing the rest of West's trump and continues with a losing diamond finesse, East will return a heart to force South's last trump. The blockage in the diamond suit means that South will be unable to return to his hand to win a third diamond trick.

After 2 rounds of trump reveal the 4-1 break, South should stop drawing trump and take a diamond finesse. It will not help East to duck his ♦K (South could then draw trump and play diamonds from the top) so East will win the trick and continue hearts for South to ruff.

South should cash a round of diamonds before drawing the rest of West's trump. Dummy's remaining blocking diamond can be discarded on the fourth round of trump. With the diamonds unblocked, South will be able to win 2 more tricks in that suit and lose only 2 club tricks at the end.

notes: West leads the ♦K against 4♠. South has 1 heart loser and up to 3 club losers if West was dealt the ♣A. On the reasonable assumption that West has the ♦A for his lead of the ♦K, the contract can be guaranteed regardless of the position of the ♣A. South should play for a loser-on-loser elimination.

South should discard a heart at trick 1, allowing West's ♦K opening lead to win the first trick. West switches to a heart and South wins the ♥K. South plays a spade to the dummy and ruffs dummy's remaining small diamond in the closed hand. South crosses back with the ♥A and ruffs dummy's last heart, eliminating that suit.

South has been careful to preserve a small spade in order to cross back to the dummy so that the ♦Q can be led for a loser-on-loser play. When East follow small, South discards a club from his hand and West wins the ♦A. West has won 2 unexpected diamond tricks, but he is now endplayed. He must either lead away from the ♣A or lead a diamond and concede a ruff and discard. In either case South will lose only 1 more club trick.

notes: West leads the ♥10 against 6NT. West is unlikely to have led from the ♥K against 6NT, but playing the ♥A is very unlikely to gain and to refuse the heart finesse would be fatal if West does have the ♥K and the ♦K is with East. In the actual layout East wins the ♥K and returns a heart to the dummy's ♥A.

The diamond finesse is required, but it would be a mistake to finesse in diamonds more than once at this stage. Suppose South crosses in clubs to take two diamond finesses. Both finesses win, but when East discards on the second round of diamonds, West's remaining diamonds stop the suit and there is no way for South to come to 12 tricks.

When West was dealt 4 (or more) diamonds to the ♦K, South's only chance is to hope that West was also dealt the sole defensive club guard. If this is the case then it is possible to squeeze West for a 12th trick.

South takes the first diamond finesse, running the ♦9. When the first finesse succeeds, that is a good sign! In order for the squeeze to mature it is necessary to run the spades before taking the second diamond finesse. When South plays the ♥Q, West is squeezed in the minors.

If West discards a diamond, South will be able to run the diamond suit after taking a second finesse. If, instead of a diamond, West discards a club on the ♥Q, South's clubs will run and it won't matter how many diamonds West was dealt (as long as he was dealt the ♦K).

Many players consider the squeeze to be a technique used only by experts. As this deal illustrates, executing a squeeze sometimes involves little more than declarer playing his winners in the proper order. All basic squeeze positions require an entry to the hand opposite the last side suit winners (South's hearts and spades in this deal). Playing a second round of diamonds too early in the play destroys this entry, making it impossible for the squeeze to succeed.
